newsitem.title: Luxembourg: EU tries to avoid Danish veto over anti-Cuba trade.
newsitem.headline: EU tries to avoid Danish veto over anti-Cuba trade.

text.p: European Union officials made a last ditch attempt on Monday to persuade Denmark against vetoing proposals to counter Washington's controversial anti-Cuba trade laws, diplomats said.
Officials said EU legal experts were closely checking bloc treaties in an effort to show Denmark that laws to counter the Helms-Burton Act will not comprise Copenhagen's sovereignty.
Denmark has said it will veto the proposed measures because it believes the part of the EU treaty they come under compromises national sovereignty.
Foreign ministers were due to vote on a response to the Helms-Burton Act -- an amalgamation of years of U.S. anti-Cuba policy -- when they met in Luxembourg on Monday.
But an immediate vote was put off until later in the day after fresh talks between Denmark, the European Commission and Ireland, the current EU president.
"The day isn't over yet," said EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan. "Denmark has displayed a welcome willingness to consider all the options."
Diplomats said a vote on the measures would now probably take place on Monday evening, unless a compromise was worked out sooner.

Officials are looking to see if the reprisal measures can be passed using another section of the EU's treaty which might provide Denmark with a way out, although one diplomat said any final response would have to include the so-called Article 235 to which Copenhagen objects.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said Copenhagen's "legal problems" remained over the article -- a catch-all clause which allows the EU to take action on behalf of the 15-nation bloc.
"We have not come to block the proposals," Petersen said. "We come to seek a solution ... but we cannot agree with it in this form."
The Danish government is currently embroiled in a court case brought by a citizens' group that accuses it of handing too much sovereignty to the EU.
But diplomats say while this would have the same effect in protecting European interests, they fear the political message they wanted to send to Washington would be diluted.

Some diplomats had been hoping to persuade Denmark at least to abstain from voting on the matter, but other diplomats said this would be "like having a nuclear deterrent made out of cardboard missiles".
Brittan said if the EU failed to come up with a response, it would send "a very bad signal" to those who wish to interfere in Europe's affairs".
The proposals would allow countersuits to be brought anywhere in Europe against litigants who sue European companies or individuals for contravening the Helms-Burton Act.

Among other things the act allows naturalised Americans to take action in U.S. courts against "traffickers" -- foreign companies or individuals accused of gaining from investments made in property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.
The Danish decision will not affect a case brought by the Commission, the EU's executive, against the United States at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Geneva.
A WTO panel is due to convene on November 20 to rule on EU complaints that the act -- and similar laws which seek to quash trade with Iran and Libya -- is extra-territorial.
The European Union is still studying proposals to bar U.S executives involved in litigation from the 15-nation bloc and has already begun compiling a "watchlist" of potential litigants.
